notes.meaning: Joshua's men brought out the five enemy rulers who had hidden inside the cave at Makkedah. The text names each city's king to highlight how great and complete the victory was. No secret hiding place can protect those who set themselves against God.

Joshua called his army leaders forward and directed them to place their feet on the necks of the fallen kings. In ancient warfare, this gesture served as a clear symbol of total victory and complete surrender. It was also an object lesson to teach the officers that the Lord would humble every proud enemy before them.

Joshua used this dramatic moment to urge his men never to be afraid or discouraged. He told them to be strong, because the Lord was going to do the very same thing to all the enemies they would face. Believers can draw courage from knowing that God goes before His people in every conflict.

Joshua struck down and executed the five kings and displayed their bodies on five trees until evening. Hanging the corpses after death was done as a solemn public warning to other rebellious cities. Joshua carefully followed God's law by removing the bodies before sundown.

At sunset, Joshua ordered the dead kings to be taken down and thrown back into the very cave where they had tried to hide. Large stones were placed over the cave mouth to seal it up. The place they had chosen for protection ended up becoming their permanent grave.

Joshua quickly marched against the city of Makkedah on that same day and took it. He put the entire city and its king to death, carrying out God's judgment just as had been done at Jericho. The rapid capture gave the enemy no time to recover or organize a defense.

From Makkedah, Joshua and all the fighting men of Israel advanced to the nearby city of Libnah. They surrounded the town and attacked it directly. Israel pressed their advantage swiftly rather than pausing to rest.

The Lord handed Libnah and its king over to Israel, and Joshua struck down everyone inside. No survivors were left in the city, and its king met the same fate as the king of Jericho. The complete defeat showed the firmness of God's holy judgment against persistent wickedness.

Joshua moved his army from Libnah to Lachish, a major fortified city. The Israelites set up their camp around it and began their siege. Even a strong walled city could not withstand an army fighting with God's help.

The Lord delivered Lachish into Israel's hands on the second day of the siege. Joshua put all the people to the sword just as he had done at Libnah. Even when a battle required extra effort, God gave the final victory to His people.

King Horam of Gezer marched out with his army to come to the aid of Lachish. Joshua met this new threat head-on and wiped out Horam and all his soldiers. Trying to defend those whom God had condemned only brought swift destruction on the king of Gezer himself.
From Lachish, Joshua and the army of Israel marched onward to Eglon. They surrounded the city and attacked its defenses. Joshua stayed focused on finishing the campaign rather than slowing down.

Israel captured Eglon on the very day they attacked it. Joshua carried out God's decree of complete destruction, striking down everyone in the city just as at Lachish. God gave His people swift success because they walked in wholehearted obedience.

Joshua and the army moved up into the mountainous region from Eglon to attack Hebron. Hebron was an ancient and famous stronghold in the hill country. The Israelites did not shrink from marching into higher, harder terrain to do God's work.

The Israelites took Hebron along with its king, its nearby towns, and all its people. Joshua left no survivors, devoting the city to destruction just as he had done at Eglon. The judgment on this major center proved that no earthly fortress can stand against God's will.

Joshua and the troops turned their attention to the city of Debir and attacked it. This fortified town in the southern hills was another important site to take. The army kept moving forward until every opposing stronghold in the south was addressed.

Israel took Debir, its ruler, and all its surrounding villages. Joshua destroyed everyone in the city, treating Debir just as he had treated Hebron and Libnah. Joshua showed steady faithfulness by completing everything the Lord commanded from start to finish.

Joshua subdued the entire southern territory, including the hills, the dry southern desert, the foothills, and the slopes. He destroyed everyone who breathed, following the clear orders of the Lord, the God of Israel. This total judgment was commanded by God because the wickedness of these nations had reached its full measure.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that biblical phrases about total destruction were common ancient battle idioms meant to describe complete military defeat and driving people out, rather than the literal slaughter of every last inhabitant.

notes.meaning: Joshua's conquest swept across the southern region from Kadesh-barnea in the south up to Gaza on the coast, and across Goshen to Gibeon. The Goshen named here was an area in southern Canaan, not the well-known region in Egypt. By taking these borders, Joshua removed the organized military power from the entire south.

Joshua conquered all these kings and their territories in a single campaign because the Lord, the God of Israel, fought for His people. The credit for this astonishing success belonged entirely to God rather than to human skill or strength. Believers find true victory only when they rely on the Lord to fight for them.

After completing the campaign, Joshua and all the Israelite forces returned to their camp at Gilgal. Gilgal was their spiritual base camp, where they had dedicated themselves to the Lord and set up memorial stones. Returning there gave the army rest and an opportunity to thank God for His deliverance.
